## Play the decision, then inspect the rules {#decision-rules-game}

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../assets/tea-decision-game.css">
<script src="../../assets/tea-decision-game.js" defer></script>
<div data-tea-decision data-locale="en">
<p>Without JavaScript, compare the three examples below. In each, you choose whether to accept a proposed split. All numbers are fictional tokens. The other player is part of the example, not a real person.</p>
<ol><li><strong>A small share for you</strong><p>Accept: you get 2; the other player gets 8. Reject: you get 0; the other player gets 0.</p><p>This is the starting rule: accepting carries out the split; rejecting gives both players zero.</p></li><li><strong>A different offer</strong><p>Accept: you get 5; the other player gets 5. Reject: you get 0; the other player gets 0.</p><p>Only the offer changed: 2–8 became 5–5. Rejecting still gives both players zero.</p></li><li><strong>A different rule for saying no</strong><p>Accept: you get 2; the other player gets 8. Reject: you get 1; the other player gets 1.</p><p>Compared with the first decision, the 2–8 offer is the same, but rejection now gives 1–1 instead of 0–0. Unallocated tokens disappear. This is a teaching variation, not the standard ultimatum game.</p></li></ol>
<p>Neither accepting nor rejecting is marked correct. Notice how the offer or rejection rule changes your options. These examples do not test personality, trustworthiness, or any effect of tea.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where this game comes from" #decision-game-notes}
The first two examples use the accept-or-reject structure of ultimatum bargaining: accepting implements the offered split; rejecting gives both players zero. The third is a teaching variation with a different rejection outcome, not the standard game. The offers are fixed examples, not research results. Real experiments may use real people and payments, so these clicks do not reproduce a study.

[Background: Güth, Schmittberger & Schwarze (1982), cited in this lesson.](#fn1)

Nothing here tests tea, warmth, or any drink. A controlled study with suitable comparisons would be needed to investigate a drink effect.
:::
<!-- decision-game:end -->

<!-- reader-guide:start -->
::: {.reader-guide}
**A question to start with**

An offer can feel generous, unfair, or risky depending on the rules around it. Start with those rules, then consider what a drink or a setting could add to the experiment.

**As you read:** Write down who moves first, what each person knows, and how the payoff works. Only then interpret a change in trust or cooperation.

## When someone else is in the room

<!-- lesson-illustration:players-and-rules:start -->
```{=html}
<figure class="tea-lesson-figure" data-lesson-illustration="players-and-rules">
  <img src="../../assets/lesson-illustrations/social-rules.svg" width="240" height="136" alt="Two players beside a token board and a rule card." loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <figcaption>Two players need more than a mood: who moves first, what each knows, and the payoff rules shape the decision. These abstract tokens do not prescribe a fair or correct move.</figcaption>
</figure>
```
<!-- lesson-illustration:players-and-rules:end -->

Sections 5.1 and 5.2 mostly watched one brain choosing alone: blurting versus checking, pumping a balloon, waiting for tomorrow. This lesson adds a second person. Trust, fairness, and cooperation are social. That is why classic laboratory games matter. They turn "will you be fair?" into something you can count, without pretending a warm mug rewrites the whole deal.

Play three scenes in your head before any formal names.

**Scene one — the unfair split.** Someone offers you $2 of a $10 pot. If you accept, you get $2 and they keep $8. If you reject, both get nothing. Cold self-interest says take the $2. Many people reject. Unfairness has a price people are willing to pay.[^1] You have seen the same instinct at a restaurant table when the bill-split feels insulting. Sometimes people walk away from a little money to punish a little disrespect.

**Scene two — the first send.** You are given $10. You may send some of it to a stranger. Whatever you send grows, and the stranger decides how much to return. Sending something is an act of **opening trust**. Getting something back is reciprocity. Sending nothing is the cold prediction. Real people often send something, at least at first.[^2]

**Scene three — cooperate or cut.** You and a partner both do better if you both cooperate. Each of you is also tempted to cut and take a short-term edge. Mutual cooperation beats mutual cutting, but the temptation is real. Cooperation needs structure and feedback, not only good vibes.[^3]

Cold theory says accept any positive crumb, send nothing, and cut. Real people often reject unfair splits, send something, and cooperate, at least in early rounds.[^1][^2][^3]

Opening trust is not the same as forever trust. That sentence will do more work than any slogan about boardroom tea service.

## Why drinks and warmth show up here

A temperature cue has been tested in an economic trust game, but the evidence is narrower than a claim about tea or lasting cooperation. In Kang et al.'s Study 1, participants briefly held a warm or cold therapeutic pack before deciding how much to invest with a computer-controlled partner. The warm group invested more on average; Study 2 did not find a significant difference in the amount invested.[^5] Neither study tested a mug, tea, fairness offers, or repeated cooperation.

Alcohol offers a separate contrast. In the cited ultimatum-game study, intoxicated participants rejected unfair offers more often than the placebo group.[^4] That result does not show what tea would do.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: the games and the evidence"}
- **Ultimatum game:** One player proposes a split; the other accepts it or both receive nothing.[^1] The alcohol study tested rejection of unfair offers.[^4]
- **Trust game:** One player sends an amount that grows; the other may return some of it.[^2] Kang et al. measured initial investments after a temperature-pack manipulation.[^5]
- **Prisoner's Dilemma:** Each player chooses whether to cooperate or defect. Repeated play can support reciprocal strategies.[^3] The warmth studies cited here did not test this game.
:::

## Play the unfair split again—with alcohol in view

Someone offers you $2 of $10. Many people reject. Now raise the alcohol. In Morewedge et al.'s design (N = 92), rejection of offers ≤20% jumped from **58.1%** to **82.4%**.[^4] Intoxication did not make people "chill about fairness." It made costly punishment *more* likely, emotional reactivity with a price tag.

That result surprises beginners who expect alcohol to make everyone say yes. Alcohol myopia narrows attention to vivid cues, and unfairness can be a vivid cue.[^8]

## Opening trust after a temperature cue

Kang et al. compared brief contact with warm and cold therapeutic packs, not drinks. In Study 1 (30 participants), the warm group invested more in a trust game; the reported difference was about **$0.15 per $1 opportunity**. Partners' responses were computer-generated. In Study 2, the investment difference was not statistically significant, although brain-activity patterns differed.[^5]

This small laboratory result cannot establish that serving tea improves negotiations or that partners will cooperate in later rounds.

## Bridge back to Chapter 4

[Chapter 4 · Section 1](../module-04/01-warmth-trust.qmd) gives the warmth evidence and its limits. Lynott et al. (2014) did not replicate Williams and Bargh's gift-choice result in a larger sample; this is a reason to avoid treating a temperature cue as a reliable social intervention.[^7]

[Chapter 4 · Section 2](../module-04/02-ritual-stress.qmd) discusses ritual and stress. It does not show that ritual changes ultimatum-game decisions. The next section explains how a study could test a drink effect directly.

## Cooperation needs a structure, not only a kettle

In repeated games, reciprocity can support cooperation when players receive feedback and expect to meet again.[^3] A warm drink has not been shown by the cited studies to change those incentives.

Serving tea has not been tested as a way to improve the opening move in these cited game studies.

## Keep the games separate

The alcohol study tested rejection of unfair offers.[^4] Kang et al. tested trust-game investments after touching packs.[^5] Axelrod examined cooperation in repeated games.[^3] These are different tasks. None measures an effect of tea on long-term cooperation.

## Story in one minute

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recap when you need it"}
Fairness, initial trust, and repeated cooperation are different decisions. The cited alcohol study concerns unfair-offer rejection; Kang et al. tested warm and cold packs before initial trust decisions. Neither tested tea.[^4][^5]
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- Check the game's rules before interpreting a decision.
- Keep the temperature-pack result separate from a claim about tea.
- Use the replication caution in [Chapter 4](../module-04/01-warmth-trust.qmd) when discussing warmth.[^7]
:::
